newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan says it pushing back invaders, rebels deny.
newsitem.headline: Sudan says it pushing back invaders, rebels deny.

text.p: The Sudanese government said on Saturday its army had pushed back attacks in the east of the country, where it says Ethiopian forces invaded last Sunday.

In Cairo the opposition National Democratic Alliance (NDA), which says it is responsible for the attacks, denied the government's account. "They are liars," opposition spokesman Farouq Abu Eissa told Reuters in Cairo.
"The armed forces have made a big advance at the battle fronts, especially in the Kurmuk and Qeissan areas," said the government newspaper al-Sudan al-Hadith.

The Sudanese government and the rebels both say the army lost Kurmuk and Qeissan, two small towns in Blue Nile state on the Ethiopian border, when the attacks began six days ago. The rebels say they have also captured army garrisons further north.

"They (the armed forces) have confined the Tigrean (Ethiopian) forces to a narrow area to the west of the towns of Kurmuk and Qeissan, forcing the Tigrean forces to retreat to rear positions," al-Sudan al-Hadith added.

The government newspaper said the Sudanese air force had bombarded areas lost by the army and that the Ethiopians were preparing to hand over their positions to south Sudanese rebels flown into Ethiopia from Uganda and Eritrea.
In Cairo the NDA said Antonov bombers of the Sudanese air force on Friday bombed a rebel-held area near the border settlement of Menze, which is also in Blue Nile state.
"The indiscriminate bombing has affected the unarmed civilians, who welcomed the revolution with enthusiasm," said a statement by the NDA's military forces.
"We appeal to the international community and humanitarian organisations to provide humanitarian assistance to the people of the area," the statement added.
In Geneva, Swiss-based Christian Solidarity International (CSI) said Antonov bombers, helicopter gunships and ground troops had been razing villages in Blue Nile state.

In the Eritrean capital Asmara, a spokesman for the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), which is part of the NDA military forces, said the Sudanese governor of Kurmuk was one of the prisoners captured when the border town fell to the rebels.
The spokesman, Yassir Arman, named him as Hussein Yaaqoub and said he was captured with some of his aides.

A private Khartoum newspaper said the prisoners included Yaaqoub Hussein, described as commissioner of Kurmuk province, and Ismail Mahmoud, the local head of the National Congress, Sudan's only legal political organisation.
The newspaper, Akhbar al-Youm, quoted Federal Rule Minister Ali al-Haj Mohammad as saying the Ethiopians took the two men away in military aircraft to an unknown destination.
Abu Eissa said other prisoners from Kurmuk were the chairman of the town council, Rabie Ahmed Kurmino, and Sheikh Qamareddin Ismail, a local dignitary.
The NDA statement named three officers -- a major and two lieutenants -- taken prisoner in the Menze area.
The focus of preparations for the army's counterattack has been Blue Nile capital Damazin, the site of the hydroelectricity plant which supplies Khartoum with 80 percent of its power.
Al-Sudan al-Hadith quoted the governor of Blue Nile state, Colonel Babaker Jaber Kabalo, as saying military reinforcements and supplies had been arriving in the state.
"The army now has the initiative on all fronts and the next few days will witness the complete destruction of the Tigrean (Ethiopian) troops," he added.

"A report from the operation areas says Ethiopian forces have begun to withdraw their military equipment as a prelude to the withdrawal of their troops," the newspaper said. The south Sudanese rebels would replace them, it added, quoting Mohammad, the federal rule minister.
There were no fresh reports on Saturday from the northern front, where Sudan says Eritrean forces have attacked. Both Eritrea and the rebels say only the rebels are attacking.
